title: I am the resurrection (John 11:1–27)
hook: Martha meets him on the road and makes her confession
carry: though he were dead, yet shall he live

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hanukkah in winter, under Solomon's porch, and hands that won't let go. Your line was no one can snatch them.

A message arrives across the Jordan from two sisters in Bethany, a village just outside Jerusalem. It's short, and it doesn't ask for anything directly: "Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick." Their brother Lazarus. John adds, so we can't miss it: "Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus." And then the strangest sentence. Right after telling us he loved them, John says that when Jesus heard Lazarus was sick, he stayed where he was two more days. John doesn't explain the wait. Not yet.

When Jesus finally says, let's go back to Judea, the disciples are alarmed: they tried to stone you there. Thomas, the one later remembered for doubting, says something brave and bleak: "Let us also go, that we may die with him." By the time they reach Bethany, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days, and friends have come from Jerusalem to comfort the sisters. Martha, hearing Jesus is near, doesn't wait at home. She goes out to meet him on the road. Her first words are honest, almost an accusation: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Then, in the same breath, she says she knows God will give him whatever he asks. Jesus says: your brother will rise again. Martha answers with a hope she already holds: "I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day." Someday. Far off. And Jesus brings it into the present tense: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live." Not, there will be a resurrection. I am. Then he asks her: believest thou this? And Martha makes her confession: "Yea, Lord: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come into the world." In Matthew's Gospel, it's Peter who says something like this. In John, it's Martha, grieving on a road, her brother four days in the tomb.
screen: then, large: `I AM THE RESURRECTION, AND THE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Martha said two things in one breath: if you had been here, and I believe; grief and faith together. Find one sentence that's true for you today, about God, or something simpler: that love matters, that people can change, that the person you lost still matters, and quietly say it out loud. If you pray, say it to God, the way Martha did; if not, say it to the room.
Martha. The sister who met Jesus on the road and heard him say, I am the resurrection, and the life.
Your line: though he were dead, yet shall he live. Grief and faith can walk the same road. Six hundred twenty-two days in.

howItsDone: Jesus's words to Martha are often read at Christian funerals; in the Book of Common Prayer burial service, they are the first words said as the body is brought to the church.

original.note: Greek: resurrection, literally a standing up again.

trapdoor: what you thought: a promise about heaven someday.
what it means: Martha believes in a resurrection far off, and Jesus says: I am the resurrection, here, now.
what a scholar hears: anastasis, standing up again; and Martha's confession echoes Peter's in Matthew.

chat.says: Can you be upset with God and still say you believe?
options: Martha said both to Jesus: if you'd been here he'd not have died, and I believe.
Martha hid her hurt from Jesus and spoke only words of faith when they met.
Martha's grief meant she couldn't believe until her brother came back to her.
chat.meaning: On the road Martha told Jesus honestly, if thou hadst been here, and in the same breath made her confession: Yea, Lord, I believe.

Bethany.meaning: a village just outside Jerusalem, home of Martha and Lazarus

Lazarus.meaning: Martha's brother, four days in the tomb

Judea.meaning: the region around Jerusalem, where they had tried to stone Jesus

Thomas.meaning: the disciple later remembered for doubting

notes: 'Many Jews of her day believed in a resurrection of the dead at the end of time' (Pharisees did; Sadducees did not). Confirm phrasing.
Burial service opening sentence 'I am the resurrection and the life' (Book of Common Prayer and many others): howItsDone says 'in many churches'. Confirm.
Hook softened in review: 'Because he loved them... he stayed' read a causal link into 11:5–6 ('therefore' in KJV 11:6 is debated); now 'Right after telling us he loved them'. Confirm.
Count of I am sayings: resurrection as fifth (bread, light, door, shepherd, resurrection). Confirm consistency.
